questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presented with a fever and constipation for 5 days. He had been nonspecifically unwell for 3 weeks. Two weeks before presentation, he had returned from a 6-month trip to India. On examination he was systemically unwell with rigors and fever >38°C. He had palpable hepatosplenomegaly and generalized abdominal tenderness. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL Platelet count 150,000/μL Blood cultures negative at 24 hours He was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone therapy.
questions.lead_in: What further investigation would have the highest diagnostic yield?

options.text: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen

questions.explanation: Bone marrow culture This patient has a suspected diagnosis of Salmonella Typhi, acquired in India, and has constipation, rather than diarrhea, seen in about 30% of patients. He has developed hepatosplenomegaly and may have bacteremia. Blood and stool cultures should be requested; blood cultures are positive in 40%–80%, stool culture positivity is 30%–40% and although not often performed, bone marrow may have additional yield >90% in more complicated cases or if unresponsive to treatment and can remain positive for >5 days after antibiotic initiation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q18

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with 3 weeks of fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, and constipation. He had returned from a 6-month trip to India 2 weeks before his symptoms began. On examination, he was confused on admission but with no focal neurology or meningism. His temperature was 39.2°C, heart rate 75 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/56 mmHg. A CT scan of the head and lumbar puncture were performed, with normal CSF findings. The CT was unremarkable. He was started empirically on intravenous ceftriaxone, fluid resuscitated, and admitted to the high dependency unit. Three malaria smears at 12-hour intervals were negative. Twenty-four hours after admission he developed worsening abdominal pain, and he had peritonitis on examination. He was taken for an exploratory laparotomy (see image). Blood cultures on admission grew gram-negative rods at 48 hours.
questions.lead_in: What part of the bowel is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation: Terminal ileum Gastrointestinal perforation, usually at the terminal ileum, is the most serious complication of typhoid infection. It manifests as an acute abdomen or as worsening of abdominal pain accompanied by shock. Perforation is associated with a high mortality risk and needs urgent surgical intervention. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q38

questions.question: Four scenarios all represent the same disease, and no patient has allergies. Scenario 1: a 13-year-old returned from Pakistan with fever and abdominal pain, gram-negative bacilli in blood at 18 hours, admitted to the PICU. Scenario 2: a 21-year-old woman returned from Thailand, unwell but hemodynamically stable. Scenario 3: a 41-year-old humanitarian worker returned from Haiti with abdominal pain, tolerating oral therapy. Scenario 4: a 17-year-old returned from Pakistan with mild abdominal pain and fever, stable, tolerating oral therapy and suitable for discharge.
questions.question_raw: 24. 4 Scenarios, all have same disease and no allergies. What is the one antimicrobial that is recommended in each situation? Scenario 1: 13 year old return from Pakistan, fever, abdo pain and GNB in blood after 18 hours, admitted to PICU. Scenario 2: 21 year old female returned from Thailand unwell but hemodynamically stable. Scenario 3: 41 year old humanitarian worker returned from Haiti with abdo pain and can tolerate oral therapy. Scenario 4: 17 year old return from Pakistan with mild abdo pain and fever and stable, can tolerate PO and be sent home.

parts.text: What is the one antimicrobial recommended in each of the four scenarios above?
Name two organisms (genus and species, taxonomically written) that can cause this disease.

parts_raw.text: What is the one antimicrobial recommended in each of the 4 scenarios above?
Name 2 organism genus and species (taxonomically written) that can cause this disease.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Scenario 1 (critically ill, Pakistan): meropenem — the 2016–2017 Pakistan outbreak strains were MDR, fluoroquinolone-resistant and ceftriaxone-resistant (XDR), and carbapenems have been used successfully for cephalosporin-resistant Salmonella Typhi. (2) Scenario 2 (Thailand, admitted, not critically ill): ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily — empirical agent of choice where reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility is common. (3) Scenario 3 (Haiti, oral therapy): ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO bid — fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility remains uncommon and sporadic outside South Asia. (4) Scenario 4 (Pakistan, mild, oral outpatient): azithromycin 500–1000 mg PO daily for 7 days — effective against MDR and fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible strains, with resistance still rare.
b) (1) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. (2) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Paratyphi A.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) ICU/critically ill from Pakistan: meropenem (XDR Salmonella Typhi — MDR, fluoroquinolone- and ceftriaxone-resistant — emerged in Pakistan in 2016–2017; carbapenems have been used successfully for cephalosporin-resistant strains). (2) Admitted, vomiting, not from Pakistan: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily. (3) Oral outpatient from Pakistan/South Asia: azithromycin 500–1000 mg PO daily × 7 days. (4) Oral outpatient from Haiti: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO bid (fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility remains sporadic outside South Asia).
b) (1) Intestinal hemorrhage — 10%–15% of hospitalized patients, usually self-limited. (2) Intestinal perforation — up to 3% of hospitalized patients, arising from Peyer patch invasion; median 9 days of fever before perforation. (Encephalopathy/confusion is also common.)
c) (1) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. (2) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Paratyphi A.

questions.model_answer:
a) Meropenem IV — XDR Salmonella Typhi (MDR, fluoroquinolone- and ceftriaxone-resistant) from the Pakistan outbreak; carbapenems have been used successfully for cephalosporin-resistant strains.
b) Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily — empirical agent of choice for severe/hospitalized enteric fever from South/Southeast Asia where reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility is common.
c) Azithromycin 500–1000 mg PO daily × 7 days — effective oral option for MDR and fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible strains, resistance still rare.
d) Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO bid — fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility is less common and sporadic outside South Asia.
e) (1) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. (2) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Paratyphi A.
f) (1) Guillain-Barré syndrome. (2) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome. (Both are listed complications of typhoid/paratyphoid fever.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell lists Guillain-Barre syndrome and hemolytic-uremic syndrome as complications but does not explicitly label them immune mediated; reactive arthritis after enteric fever is described in the enteric-infection/reactive-arthritis literature rather than this chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) Salmonella enterica (subspecies enterica) serovar Typhi.
b) (1) Meropenem IV — travel to Pakistan raises the likelihood of XDR Salmonella Typhi (MDR plus fluoroquinolone and third-generation cephalosporin resistance, as in the 2016–2017 Pakistan outbreak); carbapenems have been used successfully for ceftriaxone-resistant strains. (2) Azithromycin 20 mg/kg PO daily × 7 days — retains activity against MDR and fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible strains with only sparse reports of resistance, has established pediatric safety, and gives lower failure and relapse rates than third-generation cephalosporins. (Ceftriaxone would be reasonable only if the isolate is shown to be ceftriaxone susceptible; fluoroquinolones should not be used empirically given >90% non-susceptibility in South Asia.)
c) (1) Intestinal perforation (up to 3% of hospitalized patients; Peyer patch invasion, peritonitis, pneumoperitoneum on radiograph in only ~50%). (2) Intestinal hemorrhage (10%–15% of hospitalized patients). Severe encephalopathy is the other classic mortality-associated complication.

questions.model_answer:
a) Meropenem IV — XDR Salmonella Typhi (MDR, fluoroquinolone- and ceftriaxone-resistant) from the 2016–2017 Pakistan outbreak; carbapenems have been used successfully for cephalosporin-resistant strains. Add high-dose dexamethasone if shock or profound encephalopathy.
b) Azithromycin 500–1000 mg (20 mg/kg) PO daily × 7 days — oral agent still active against XDR/MDR and fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible strains.
c) Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily (7–14 days, at least 7 days after defervescence) — empirical choice for severe enteric fever where reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility is common.
d) Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO bid × 5–7 days if acquired outside South Asia (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America), where fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility is sporadic; use azithromycin instead for South Asian acquisition.
e) Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi.
f) (1) Intestinal perforation (up to 3% of hospitalized patients). (2) Intestinal hemorrhage (10%–15% of hospitalized patients). Others: severe encephalopathy/seizures, jaundice/hepatitis, myocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis.

cohort_answer.text: Pakistan sick: Meropenem. Pakistan not sick: Azithromycin. Non-Pakistan sick: Ceftriaxone. Non-Pakistan not sick: FQ (e.g. cipro) for Sub-Saharan Africa or Azithromycin for South Asia (due to increasing resistance in Asia). Bacteria: Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. Complications: Aortitis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, bacteremia, gastroenteritis, bowel perforation, septic joint. (XDR typhoid reported in Iraq, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan - majority from Pakistan; azithromycin typically still susceptible for XDR strains.)
